I'll work through each draft carefully, applying only the five structural tests and the gate test.

**Ch 012 draft review:**

The draft is well-compressed. I check for dangling pronouns, broken pivots, missing glosses, etc. One candidate:

- "He chose to appear as a free talker, who loathed pomposity and enjoyed a joke; but how much was nature and how much was mask, he was himself too simple a nature to know." — The source set this up with "At table, among friends, Mr. Seward threw off restraint, or seemed to throw it off… in the world he threw it off, like a politician, for effect. In both cases he chose to appear…" The draft cuts the two-sided setup but the sentence still parses — the reader understands Seward chose to appear this way. Not a structural failure.

- "This might be a commonplace of 1900, but in 1860 it was paradox. The Southern statesmen were regarded as standards of statesmanship, and such standards barred education. To this school, Henry Adams had come for a new education, although the Sioux Indians would have taught less mischief." — Source had an intervening sentence about Sumner's offense being his insistence on Southern ignorance, and a sentence about "He stood a living proof of it. To this school…" The draft cuts these and the "although" clause then reads as a broken pivot — but actually "although the Sioux Indians…" contrasts with "come for a new education," and the source's deleted Sumner sentence was just explanatory color. The matrix still parses.

- "The whole field of instruction south of the Potomac was shut off" — source introduced this with "No one learned a useful lesson from the Confederate school except to keep away from it. Thus, at one sweep…" The draft cuts this and goes straight to "The whole field of instruction south of the Potomac was shut off." This is abrupt but the preceding sentences about cotton-planters establish the south-of-Potomac context. A reader can follow.

- "Study it as one might, the hope of education narrowed itself to the possible influence of only two men—Sumner and Seward." Source had "till the arrival of the President-elect." Draft drops this qualifier. Still parses fine.

- The paragraph beginning "Only one man in Adams's reach seemed to him supremely fitted…" is followed immediately by "He had necessarily followed Seward and his father…" In the source, these are separated by a paragraph about going over the experience, struggling to see where he blundered, and making acquaintances. The draft's transition is abrupt but both sentences parse independently.

Ch 012 draft appears structurally coherent.

**Ch 013 draft review:**

- "By way of teaching him quickly, they sent out their new Minister to Russia in the same ship: Cassius M. Clay, a teacher having no equal though possibly some rivals." — The pronoun "they" has no antecedent in the draft. The source's preceding context had "Secretary Seward had occasion to learn the merits of Cassius M. Clay in the diplomatic service, but Mr. Seward's education profited less than the private secretary's, Cassius Clay as a teacher having no equal." In the draft, the paragraph before this sentence ends with "No young man, not in Government pay, could draw from such lessons any confidence in himself" — wait, actually the draft order is: the Cassius Clay sentence comes *before* the "No young man" sentence. Let me re-read the draft.

Draft order: "By way of teaching him quickly, they sent out their new Minister to Russia in the same ship: Cassius M. Clay, a teacher having no equal though possibly some rivals. No young man, not in Government pay, could draw from such lessons any confidence in himself."

"They" — who? The preceding paragraph ends: "He thought it right to play the adventurer as his father and grandfather had done before him, without a murmur." Before that: the young man felt betrayal; the private secretary's stature insufficient. No "they" antecedent exists in the draft. In the source, the prior paragraph ends similarly but the "they" arguably refers to the Government/Administration — the source's "they sent out" also has a somewhat loose referent, but in the source the full paragraph context makes clear it's the Government (having just described the Government sending Adams out as adventurer). In the draft this context is preserved — the preceding paragraph does discuss the Government sending Adams out ("the Government should send him out as an adventurer"). So "they" = the Government, which is present in the draft. A competent reader can infer this. Marginal but probably not a genuine confusion.

- "Then came the Trent Affair: the seizure of Mason and Slidell brought the Legation to the brink of war, and the Minister, summoned from Yorkshire, met the crisis without losing his nerve." — "summoned from Yorkshire" — Yorkshire has not been established anywhere in this draft chapter. The source chapter also does not establish Yorkshire in the material before this sentence; this sentence appears at the very end of the source chapter as a closing paragraph. So Yorkshire is introduced here in both source and draft without prior establishment. This is equally unexplained in source and draft — not a compression artifact.

- "The shock passed; the secretaries learned that patience, silence, and the closing of newspaper indiscretions were the only diplomacy left to them." — "the secretaries" — plural. In the draft, only one secretary (Henry) has been mentioned. The source similarly uses "the secretaries" here. In the source, Charley Wilson (Secretary of Legation) was named, providing a basis for plural "secretaries." In the draft, Wilson is mentioned only as "The Secretary of Legation was the editor of a Chicago newspaper who had applied for the Chicago Post-Office, with no thought of staying." Wilson is authorized to be cut (he's on the minor-character removal list), but the draft actually retained the reference to him (anonymously). Still, "the secretaries" could confuse — but a reader knows a legation has multiple secretaries; this is not genuinely confusing.

- "That Mr. Adams was unfit might well be, since it was hard to find a fit appointment except Sumner himself; the weakest of Mr. Adams's proofs of fitness was his consent to quit a safe seat in Congress for an exceedingly unsafe seat in London." — The source has: "the weakest of all Mr. Adams's proofs of fitness was his consent to quit a safe seat in Congress for an exceedingly unsafe seat in London with no better support than Senator Sumner, at the head of the Foreign Relations Committee, was likely to give him." The draft drops "with no better support than Senator Sumner… was likely to give him." The source's version explained *why* London was unsafe — Sumner (as Foreign Relations Chairman) would not support him. The draft just says "exceedingly unsafe seat in London" without explaining why unsafe relative to Congress. But the draft reader understands: Adams is going into a diplomatic crisis without support. This is less ornamented, not structurally broken.

The Ch 013 draft is also structurally coherent.
